17 A man of mass 75 kg runs up a staircase consisting of 30 steps. Each step is 20 cm high.
The man takes a time of 7.0 s to run from the bottom of the staircase to the top.
What is the average rate of increase of gravitational potential energy of the man?
A
64 W
B
450 W
C
630 W
D
4400 W

hints: First find the total vertical height climbed from 30 steps of $20 \text{ cm}$ each, converting centimetres to metres.
Recall that gain in gravitational potential energy is $\Delta E_p = mgh$ with $m = 75 \text{ kg}$ and $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Average rate of increase means power $P = \Delta E_p / t$, so divide your energy in joules by $t = 7.0 \text{ s}$ to get watts.
walkthrough: Total vertical height is number of steps times height per step: $h = 30 \times 20 \text{ cm} = 600 \text{ cm} = 6.0 \text{ m}$.
Gain in gravitational potential energy is $\Delta E_p = mgh$.
Substitute $m = 75 \text{ kg}$, $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $h = 6.0 \text{ m}$: $\Delta E_p = 75 \times 9.81 \times 6.0 \approx 4415 \text{ J}$.
Average rate is power: $P = \Delta E_p / t = 4415 / 7.0 \approx 631 \text{ W}$, which is about $630 \text{ W}$ with correct units of $\text{J s}^{-1} = \text{W}$.
This is option C. Option D forgets the division by time, while A and B are far too small.

A.explanation: This is about $64 \text{ W}$, which is $mh/t$ without $g$. Gravitational potential energy gain must include weight $mg$, not just mass times height.

B.explanation: This $450 \text{ W}$ is too small. The total gain $mgh$ is about $4400 \text{ J}$, and dividing by $7.0 \text{ s}$ gives a much larger rate near $630 \text{ W}$.

C.explanation: Total height $6.0 \text{ m}$ gives $\Delta E_p = mgh \approx 4410 \text{ J}$, and $4410/7.0 \approx 630 \text{ W}$.

D.explanation: This $4400 \text{ W}$ is the total energy gain $mgh$ in joules, forgetting to divide by the $7.0 \text{ s}$ time to get the rate in watts.
